title: Fabricated scientists and studies. Court imposes Estonia's first AI fine for AI hallucinations

reading.body:
This is a hallucination failure in a document-drafting context: a generative model produced citations to researchers and studies that do not exist, and those citations were carried into a legal filing without being verified. The failure surfaced at the point of submission, when the court could not locate the cited material. The system was used to prepare a formal complaint, a setting where every factual assertion is checkable against public records.

Catching it required only a lookup. The cited Estonian researchers and their studies could have been searched before filing, and the court itself performed that check after the fact. The court's own account places responsibility on the user rather than the tool, and notes that AI use in filings is permitted but that each submission still needs full review, which slows proceedings.

What is not established is how the plaintiffs used the tool, what they asked it, or whether they knew the citations were fabricated. The plaintiffs said they had not meant to mislead, and the court's penalty rested on false claims submitted knowingly or through gross negligence, not on a finding of intent.

summary:
A Tallinn court fined ten plaintiffs after they submitted a legal filing citing academic sources that did not exist. The plaintiffs were challenging a logging permit and referenced studies on clearcutting, but the court found the cited Estonian researchers were not real and the studies could not be found. The court gave them a chance to provide the studies and warned of penalties, and the plaintiffs said they had not meant to mislead. One plaintiff was fined 150 euros and nine others 50 euros each.

The court said AI use is allowed but users are responsible for accuracy, since AI can produce false information. Court chair Kaupo Kruusvee said AI use in filings is growing and can slow proceedings because every submission still needs full review. He said courts do not use AI to draft decisions. Under Estonian law, courts may fine parties who submit false claims knowingly or through gross negligence.
